intents.title: Intents
intents.desc: An intent says what a component means. A variant says how loudly it says it. `intent` appears on 34 components, and it is the prop that decides whether a user reads something as routine, as worth pausing over, or as a point of no return — so it is worth getting exactly right.
intents.vocab_desc: Every intent resolves through `tokens/intents.json`, so these meanings are the same wherever the prop appears.
intents.primary_means: This is the main thing on this surface
intents.primary_use: One element per screen carries the eye. Marking a second one does not make either more important — it makes both ordinary.
intents.success_means: Something completed, and nothing further is required
intents.success_use: The work is finished. A state that is merely healthy or in progress is not success; it is `default`.
intents.info_means: Context the user did not ask for but benefits from
intents.info_use: The message adds background. If ignoring it costs the user nothing, this is the intent.
intents.warning_means: You can proceed, but check first
intents.warning_use: The action will succeed and can be undone or corrected afterwards.
intents.danger_use: Deleting, revoking, overwriting, sending. Also the state a form field is in when the value is invalid.
intents.neutral_use: The label is real and carries no urgency — a status of `Draft`, a count, a tag.
intents.boundary_title: The line between warning and danger
intents.boundary_desc: This is the pair that gets confused, and the test is not how bad the outcome feels — it is whether the user can get back. If the action can be undone, it is a warning. If it cannot, it is danger. Leaving a form with unsaved edits is a warning: the edits are still there until the user confirms. Deleting the record is danger: nothing brings it back. Spending `danger` on recoverable situations is what makes it stop working — by the time a genuinely irreversible action appears, the user has learned that red means nothing in particular.
intents.default_title: default and neutral are not the same thing
intents.default_desc: Both are colourless, and that is where the resemblance ends. Measured against the source: `default` resolves to no colour and no surface at all — it paints nothing, because no intent has been applied. `neutral` resolves to no colour but a complete surface — a grey fill, a text colour, a subtle tint. It paints, deliberately, in grey. So `default` is the absence of an intent, while `neutral` is an intent whose meaning is "no emphasis". Using `neutral` to mean "I did not pick one" produces grey chrome that nobody chose.
intents.family_title: The vocabulary depends on the component
intents.family_desc: There is no single list. Five intent types exist, each a deliberate subset of the six meanings, because not every component can meaningfully say every one of them. Which type a component takes is visible in its props.
intents.family_button_why: No `primary`. A button's importance is carried by its variant, not its intent — `solid` is the prominent one. Putting hierarchy in both places would give you two ways to say the same thing, and they would disagree.
intents.family_indicator_why: No `default`. A badge always paints something, so "apply no intent" has nothing to mean; the uncoloured option is `neutral`, which paints grey on purpose.
intents.family_feedback_why: No `primary` and no `neutral`. An alert either carries a meaning or is left uncoloured — colour here is opt-in, and an alert that is emphatically grey is not a thing worth expressing.
intents.family_field_why: Two values only. A field is either fine or it is not. There is no useful middle state to paint, and a field that is `warning` yellow while still accepting input tells the user nothing actionable.
intents.avoid_title: What not to do with intent
intents.avoid_1: Do not let colour be the only carrier
intents.avoid_1_desc: Intent resolves to colour. A user who cannot distinguish the hues gets nothing from it. Every intent that matters needs a word, an icon, or a position that says the same thing — WCAG 1.4.1 is the floor, not the goal.
intents.avoid_2: Do not reach for a value the family does not have
intents.avoid_2_desc: If a button seems to need `warning`, the button is not the problem — the surrounding copy is doing too little. Widening the type to fit one screen removes the constraint that keeps every other screen consistent.
intents.avoid_3: Do not use intent for hierarchy
intents.avoid_3_desc: `secondary` was removed for exactly this reason: it was a hierarchy word sitting in a vocabulary of meanings, and it painted the same grey as `neutral`. Loudness belongs to the variant.
intents.avoid_4: Do not carry an intent through a whole screen
intents.avoid_4_desc: Intents mark exceptions. When a screen is mostly coloured, nothing on it is marked — the exception has become the background.
intents.variant_desc: The two props answer different questions and compose freely: intent picks the hue, variant decides how much of the surface that hue claims. `intent="danger" variant="subtle"` is a quiet destructive marker; `intent="danger" variant="solid"` is the same meaning demanding attention. Choose the intent from what is true, then the variant from how much room the message deserves.
intents.family_stepper_why: Not part of the intent system at all. `Stepper` uses the name `intent` for step states, and its values share nothing with the six meanings — `error` is the one that comes close, and even it is spelled differently from `danger`. Read the type before assuming a component speaks this vocabulary.
intents.family_note: Five of these are generated from `tokens/intents.json`, so they cannot drift from the token values. `StepperIntent` is hand-written outside that source.
